How to Combine Assignment Scores with Different Point Totals

Combine marks from unequal assignment totals correctly, compare pooled points with equal percentages, and check the syllabus before averaging.

By GradeTargetCalc · Published 2 November 2026 · 5 min read

In this guide
Choose the grading rule before combining marksBuild two columns with the same eligible assignmentsAdd earned points and possible points separatelyExplain why the result is closer to the large projectAdding a new assignment changes both totalsPool inside a category before applying its course weightCheck exclusions and communicate the calculation clearlyFAQsSources
01

Choose the grading rule before combining marks

An eight-point worksheet and a hundred-point project may appear as neighboring rows in a gradebook, but that does not mean they carry equal influence. Before averaging their percentages, establish whether the course pools their raw points, gives each assignment equal importance or assigns separate weights.

This guide follows a pooled-points rule. Under that rule, every available point in the selected pool has equal numerical value. An assessment offering more points therefore contributes more to the final fraction. A different syllabus rule needs a different calculation even when the underlying marks are identical.

02

Build two columns with the same eligible assignments

List earned marks in one column and possible marks in the other. Use the awarded values, including valid partial credit, rather than rounded percentages copied from a dashboard. Both columns must cover exactly the same assessments and reporting period.

For an example, use a worksheet scored 6/8, a short report scored 21/30 and a project scored 84/100. The individual percentages are 75%,70% and 84%, but keep the original fractions. They preserve the relative point totals that the pooling rule requires. Mark ungraded work separately until you know how it belongs in the calculation.

03

Add earned points and possible points separately

Combined percentage = Sum of earned points ÷ Sum of possible points ×100. For the example, earned marks total 6+21+84=111. Possible marks total 8+30+100=138. The pooled grade is 111÷138×100=80.4347…%, displayed as approximately 80.43%.

Do not add the three percentage values and divide by three unless the assignments count equally. That method gives(75+70+84)÷3=76.33…%. Its lower result is not a contradiction: it gives the small worksheet as much influence as the larger project, changing the intended weighting.

04

Explain why the result is closer to the large project

The project carries 100 of the 138 available points, about 72.46% of this pool. The report carries about 21.74%, and the worksheet about 5.80%. Those proportions explain why the combined percentage sits closer to 84% than to 70%. They are effective shares within this selected pool, not necessarily course-category weights.

You can verify the answer by treating each percentage as weighted by its possible marks. The weighted sum is 75×8+70×30+84×100=11,100; dividing by 138 gives the same 80.4347…%. This alternative check works because each percentage was derived from the matching earned and possible values.

05

Adding a new assignment changes both totals

Suppose you later earn 17/20 on another eligible assignment. The new pool is 128 earned out of 158 possible, or 81.0126…%. You cannot simply add 17 to the old numerator while leaving 138 as the denominator, because the new assignment adds available points as well as earned points.

A recorded zero on that same twenty-point assignment produces 111/158, approximately 70.25%. Excluding an ungraded assignment leaves 111/138 instead. These are different records, so the large difference must be resolved through assignment status and policy rather than choosing whichever percentage seems more plausible.

06

Pool inside a category before applying its course weight

Sometimes raw points are pooled within a homework category that represents only part of the course. If the initial 111/138 pool belongs to homework worth 20% of the course, its 80.4347…% category average contributes approximately 16.08696 course percentage points. Other categories must supply the remaining contributions.

Do not combine homework raw points with exam raw points if the syllabus assigns those categories different percentages. A hundred-point exam may have a specified 40% course share regardless of how many homework points are available. First calculate each category using its own rule, then combine category percentages using the course weights.

07

Check exclusions and communicate the calculation clearly

Before relying on the total, check whether any assignment is dropped, excused, capped, excluded from the grade or governed by an extra-credit rule. Each change can alter the eligible numerator, denominator or both. A score above its normal maximum also needs an explicit policy; our standard percentage tool rejects earned points above possible points.

A useful result record states“111 earned from 138 possible points across these three graded assignments,” rather than presenting 80.43% without context. Keep your worksheet so a future assignment can be added consistently and a discrepancy can be reproduced.

  • Use raw awarded marks before rounding to percentages.
  • Include each eligible assignment once in both columns.
  • Separate pending work from awarded zeros.
  • Pool only the assessments the course treats as one points group.
Quick answers

Frequently asked questions

Can I average the displayed percentages instead?

Only when the assignments are supposed to count equally. Pooled points preserve unequal possible totals; a simple percentage average gives each assignment one equal share.

Should I round each percentage first?

Prefer the original earned and possible marks. Rounding individual percentages before combining can introduce unnecessary error, particularly near a reporting boundary.

Does a pooled homework grade equal my course grade?

Only if that pool represents the whole course. Otherwise apply its category weight and combine it with the other category contributions.
